nameStory: The pear-shaped puffball gets its name from its distinctive bulbous shape that resembles an upside-down pear, complete with a narrowed 'neck' at the base. It's also called the stump puffball because of its habit of growing directly on decaying wood stumps and logs, unlike most puffballs that prefer soil.
description: The pear-shaped puffball is a small, white to tan mushroom that looks like a tiny balloon attached to wood. When young, it's smooth and white, but as it matures, it develops a small opening at the top that releases dusty brown spores when disturbed. These charming little fungi typically grow in dense clusters on rotting logs and stumps, making them easy to spot once you know where to look. They're usually about 1-3 inches tall and equally wide at the bulbous top.

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly pear-shaped with a bulbous top tapering to a narrower base, often with visible white root-like threads (mycelium) connecting it to the wood

idTips.label: Surface
idTips.description: Smooth when young, becoming slightly bumpy with age; feels like soft leather when fresh, papery when mature

idTips.label: Spores
idTips.description: Mature specimens release olive-brown to dark brown dusty spores through a small opening at the top when pressed or disturbed

idTips.label: Interior
idTips.description: When cut open, young specimens are pure white inside like marshmallow, turning yellow then brown as spores develop

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, pleasant mushroomy smell; older ones may smell earthy or slightly unpleasant

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows directly on decaying wood in tight clusters of dozens of individuals, never found on soil alone

habitat: Look for pear-shaped puffballs on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches throughout New England's forests. They're especially common on rotting maple, oak, and birch wood in both dense forests and edge habitats. You'll often find them in the same spots year after year, as they return to feed on the same decaying wood sources.

seasonality.spring: Early clusters may begin appearing on logs as temperatures warm, especially after spring rains on wood that's been decomposing through winter.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for fresh, white specimens perfect for identification. Look for dense clusters after summer thunderstorms on partially shaded logs.
seasonality.fall: Still actively fruiting through autumn, though many specimens will be releasing brown spores by this time. Great season for spotting their distinctive pear shape.
seasonality.winter: Old, dried specimens may persist on logs as papery brown shells, but fresh fruiting is rare in cold weather.

funFact: This little puffball is actually a world traveler that has colonized every continent except Antarctica, making it one of the most cosmopolitan fungi on Earth - all by hitching rides on decaying wood that humans transport around the globe!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small puffballs, but the pear-shaped puffball is the only one that grows directly on wood rather than soil. If you find small puffballs growing from the ground, they're a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Lycoperdon to its own special genus Apioperdon in 2017, making it the sole member of its genus - a taxonomic VIP with no close relatives.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus, compare it to other puffballs in the family. Unlike giant puffballs that can grow massive and round, or earthball puffballs with their warty surfaces, the pear-shaped puffball stays small and maintains its distinctive teardrop profile. Most importantly, it's the only common puffball that exclusively grows on wood rather than soil.
